verses.text: What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don't they come from the passions at war within you?
You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask.
And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures.
You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think the Scripture says without reason that the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns with envy?
But He gives us more grace. This is why it says: "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble."
Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.

Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it.
There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
Come now, you who say, "Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit."
You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.
Instead, you ought to say, "If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that."
As it is, you boast in your proud intentions. All such boasting is evil.
Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin.

context.author: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (1:1). Tradition identifies him with James the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem.
context.genre: Letter with the feel of wisdom literature and a sermon
context.audience: Probably Jewish Christians living outside the land of Israel (“the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” 1:1). Some take the phrase as a title for all of God's people.
context.mapLabel: QUARRELS AND THE FRIEND OF THE WORLD
context.setting: James asks where wars and fights come from and answers: from desires waging war within. He calls friendship with the world enmity with God, and urges his readers to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, and humble themselves. Then he warns against judging a brother and against boasting about tomorrow.
context.custom: The prophets described Israel's unfaithfulness to God as adultery (Hosea 2:2-5), and James uses that picture for believers who befriend the world (v.4). Merchants of the day planned trips of a year to make a profit (v.13), and James says that life is a mist.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 5 warns the rich and encourages patience and prayer.
context.timelineBible: James quotes Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (v.6). A mist that appears for a little while echoes Psalm 39:5-6 and Hosea 13:3.
context.sparkNotes: What causes quarrels among you? Is it not your passions at war within you? You ask and do not receive because you ask wrongly. Friendship with the world is enmity with God. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Submit yourselves to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Do not speak evil against one another. Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city.” You are a mist. Instead say, “If the Lord is willing.”

translation.meaning: Vapor or steam. Life is brief.

otBackground.note: Quoted in James 4:6 in its Greek form. The Hebrew speaks of scoffers and of favor for the humble.
All flesh is grass and quickly fades. Compare the mist of James 4:14.
Israel's unfaithfulness pictured as adultery. Compare James 4:4.

overview.summary: Conflicts come from selfish desires. James calls for humility, submission to God, and drawing near to him, and warns against judging and presumptuous plans.

history.t: James traces fights among believers to desires that war inside them (4:1-3) and warns against speaking against one another (4:11-12). He does not say what the fights were about.

James imagines traders who say they will go to a city, spend a year there, do business and make a profit (4:13). Roman roads and Mediterranean sea routes made such journeys common for people with money to risk.

customs.t: The Greek word atmis means vapor, steam or smoke. Hosea 13:3 uses similar pictures for things that quickly vanish: morning mist, early dew, chaff and smoke. James says that life is like this (4:14).
To cleanse the hands and purify the heart, and to be wretched, mourn and weep (4:8-9), is the language of repentance in the prophets (Isaiah 1:15-17; Joel 2:12-13).
The prophets often described Israel's unfaithfulness to God as adultery (Hosea 2:2-5; Jeremiah 3:6-10; Ezekiel 16). James uses the same picture for believers who make friends with the world.

archaeology.t: Wrecks and cargoes on the Mediterranean seabed show how much trade moved by sea in Roman times. A fresco of the merchant ship Isis Giminiana, about AD 200-250, is in the Vatican Museums.
The synagogue at Ostia, the port of Rome, shows that Jewish communities lived in the trading cities of the Mediterranean. James names no city, but his readers lived in settings like these.

overview.discussion: James says “You do not have, because you do not ask.” What am I trying to get by my own effort that I have never asked God for?
overview.book: The letter of James · 5 chapters. Brisk, practical teaching in the tradition of Proverbs and the Sermon on the Mount.
overview.author: James

historicalImage.caption: A Roman fresco of a merchant ship named the Isis Giminiana, now in the Vatican Museums (about AD 200-250). It is later than James, but it shows a cargo ship of the kind that carried traders around the Mediterranean. James 4:13 pictures merchants who say they will go to a city, spend a year there and make a profit.

currentImage.caption: Antakya in Turkey, the modern city on the site of ancient Antioch on the Orontes, a large city of Roman Syria with many Jews. James does not say where his readers lived, and Antioch is only one suggestion. In 4:13 he pictures merchants who plan to go to a city, spend a year there and make a profit.
